control_description: Conduct an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality integrity and availability of ePHI.
pharmacy_context: Pharmacy Management System (PMS) insurance billing workstations fax servers and email systems handling refill requests must be in scope. Drive-thru audio systems that capture patient names are often overlooked.
assessment_question: Has the organization completed a documented Risk Analysis covering all systems that create receive maintain or transmit ePHI?
evidence_example: Risk Analysis report dated within 12 months; asset inventory; threat/vulnerability list; risk rating matrix
evidence_description: Risk Analysis was last performed in 2022. No updated inventory of new insurance clearinghouse or drive-thru audio system.
finding_notes: Outdated RA; new systems not in scope. OCR has cited lack of current RA in 70% of breach settlements.

control_description: Implement security measures sufficient to reduce identified risks and vulnerabilities to a reasonable and appropriate level.
pharmacy_context: High-risk items in pharmacy: shared workstation logins lack of workstation auto-lock unencrypted backup drives containing patient profiles.
assessment_question: Is there a Risk Management plan that documents how identified risks are mitigated transferred or accepted?
evidence_example: Risk Management action plan; POs for encryption software; policy memos on workstation timeout settings
evidence_description: Risk Management plan exists but is not tracked to completion. 12 open risks from 2022 have no owners or dates.
finding_notes: Risk register exists but is static. No quarterly review meetings. Risks are identified then forgotten.

control_description: Apply appropriate sanctions against workforce members who fail to comply with the security policies.
pharmacy_context: Technicians accessing patient profiles without a valid prescription (curiosity browsing) must trigger documented disciplinary steps.
assessment_question: Are workforce sanctions for security violations defined in policy and enforced consistently?
evidence_example: Sanction policy in Employee Handbook; documented case (redacted) of policy enforcement
evidence_description: Sanction policy exists in handbook but no documented enforcement cases in last 24 months despite known incidents.
finding_notes: Two technicians were verbally warned for curiosity browsing but no written documentation exists. Policy lacks teeth.

control_description: Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity.
pharmacy_context: Most retail pharmacies rely on PMS vendor logs (e.g. QS/1 PioneerRx). Verify someone is assigned to review them monthly not just after an incident.
assessment_question: Are audit logs from PMS firewall and Active Directory reviewed on a defined schedule?
evidence_example: Log review schedule; last 3 months of review sign-off sheets; SIEM/ticketing tickets
evidence_description: PMS logs are stored but no one is assigned to review them. Firewall logs are enabled but not reviewed.
finding_notes: No log review SOP. No SIEM. Post-breach forensic analysis would be the first time logs are examined.

control_description: Identify the security official responsible for developing and implementing security policies.
pharmacy_context: In a retail pharmacy this is often the Pharmacy Manager or PIC (Pharmacist in Charge). For multi-store chains a District-level Security Officer may be designated.
assessment_question: Is a Security Officer/Privacy Officer formally designated in writing with current contact information?
evidence_example: Job description or policy document naming the Security Officer; org chart
evidence_description: Pharmacy Manager Maria Chen is designated as Security Officer and Privacy Officer in the Employee Handbook and on the org chart.
finding_notes: Designation is current. Contact info is posted in break room and shared drive. Annual review is scheduled.

control_description: Implement procedures to ensure all workforce members have appropriate access to ePHI and prevent those without access.
pharmacy_context: Float technicians covering multiple stores should not retain perpetual access to all store PMS instances; access should mirror active schedule.
assessment_question: Are workforce access levels reviewed and documented during onboarding role changes and termination?
evidence_example: Access request forms; role-change tickets; termination checklist including IT access revocation
evidence_description: Access is provisioned during onboarding but quarterly access reviews are not performed. Float techs retain old store access.
finding_notes: Float technician Jamal still has active PMS credentials for Store 4421 despite not working there since January.

control_description: Implement procedures for authorizing and supervising workforce members who work with ePHI.
pharmacy_context: PRN/on-call technicians and immunizing pharmacists from staffing agencies need background checks and signed BAA/NDA before system credentials are issued.
assessment_question: Is there a documented authorization workflow before a new hire or contractor gets ePHI access?
evidence_example: Background check results (retention only); signed confidentiality agreements; manager approval emails
evidence_description: All new hires require PIC approval background check and signed confidentiality agreement before IT creates accounts.
finding_notes: Process is followed consistently. Last exception was a temp tech in 2024 who was denied access pending background check.

control_description: Establish procedures to determine that a workforce member's access to ePHI is appropriate.
pharmacy_context: Cashiers should not have read access to patient medication histories; inventory clerks should not have prescriber DEA override capabilities.
assessment_question: Are access rights tied to job roles (RBAC) with documented minimum necessary justifications?
evidence_example: Role-based access matrix; least-privilege review meeting minutes
evidence_description: RBAC is configured in PMS but not documented. Minimum necessary justifications are verbal not written.
finding_notes: The PIC knows who gets what but there is no written RBAC matrix. An OCR auditor would see ad-hoc access decisions.

control_description: Implement procedures for terminating access when employment ends.
pharmacy_context: Retail turnover is high. A technician fired for theft who still has PMS credentials at midnight is a breach waiting to happen.
assessment_question: Is IT access revoked within 24 hours of termination? Are physical keys/badge access revoked concurrently?
evidence_example: Termination ticket timestamps; last-login audit for termed employees; badge deactivation logs
evidence_description: IT access is revoked within 48 hours on average. Physical badge deactivation is manual and takes 3-5 days.
finding_notes: Last termination (May 10) had PMS access revoked in 36 hours but badge was active for 4 days.

control_description: Implement policies and procedures for authorizing access to ePHI based on workforce roles.
pharmacy_context: Per HIPAA minimum necessary a technician filling prescriptions needs the patient's med history; a delivery driver scanning 'ready for pickup' only needs name and status—not diagnosis.
assessment_question: Does a formal Access Authorization Policy exist require management approval and get reviewed annually?
evidence_example: Access Authorization Policy; annual review sign-off; exception request log
evidence_description: No formal Access Authorization Policy exists. Access is granted by verbal PIC approval and IT ticket without written justification.
finding_notes: All access changes are tracked in IT tickets but there is no policy requiring management sign-off or annual review.

control_description: Establish procedures for granting access to ePHI based on workforce roles.
pharmacy_context: New pharmacist intern credentials should require PIC approval and have an expiration date aligned with internship end date.
assessment_question: Are access provisioning workflows documented and do they include approval before system accounts are created?
evidence_example: Access request workflow diagram; sample approved access request; provisioning SOP
evidence_description: Provisioning workflow exists in IT ticketing system but is not documented as a formal SOP. Intern accounts do not auto-expire.
finding_notes: Intern accounts require manual calendar reminders. Two past interns had active credentials for 6 weeks post-internship.

control_description: Implement procedures to modify access when workforce roles change.
pharmacy_context: A technician promoted to inventory specialist loses dispensing-floor access but gains purchasing/vendor portal access. Dual access should not persist indefinitely.
assessment_question: When employees are promoted transferred or change departments is their ePHI access reviewed and adjusted?
evidence_example: Role-change access review form; quarterly access recertification list
evidence_description: No role-change access review process exists. When staff change roles their old access is often not removed.
finding_notes: Technician promoted to inventory clerk in March still has full dispensing access and can view patient profiles.

control_description: Implement procedures to document access requests establishment modification and termination.
pharmacy_context: PMS audit logs often capture the action but the *business justification* is stored in HR or IT ticketing. Both are needed for an OCR investigation.
assessment_question: Is there an audit trail of all access changes (who what when why) retained for at least 6 years?
evidence_example: 6-year access change log; ticketing system export (redacted); PMS user audit report
evidence_description: Access changes are logged in IT tickets but business justifications are not consistently captured. Retention is 3 years not 6.
finding_notes: Ticketing system auto-purges tickets after 3 years. No archive policy exists for access-related tickets.

control_description: Implement a security awareness and training program for all workforce members.
pharmacy_context: Retail pharmacies use high-turnover staff. Training must be part of Day-1 onboarding not just annual refreshers.
assessment_question: Is annual HIPAA Security training mandatory for all workforce members including contractors and volunteers?
evidence_example: Training curriculum; LMS completion reports; new-hire training checklists
evidence_description: Annual HIPAA Security training is mandatory. Day-1 onboarding includes a 30-minute security module. Completion is tracked in LMS.
finding_notes: All 14 current staff completed 2025 training. Two new hires completed Day-1 module in April.

control_description: Periodic security updates and reminders.
pharmacy_context: Pharmacies see seasonal staff spikes (flu season back-to-school). Timely reminders about suspicious refill-request emails are high-value.
assessment_question: Are security reminders (e.g. phishing password hygiene tailgating) sent at least quarterly?
evidence_example: Quarterly reminder emails; bulletin board posters; phishing simulation results
evidence_description: Security reminders are sent quarterly via email but not tracked for read receipts. No phishing simulations have been run.
finding_notes: Last phishing awareness email was March 2026. No simulation has been conducted to measure click-through rates.

control_description: Protection from malicious software procedures.
pharmacy_context: Many pharmacy workstations still run Windows 10 and rely on free AV or nothing. PMS terminals connected to the internet for insurance adjudication are high-risk.
assessment_question: Is anti-malware deployed on all endpoints that touch ePHI? Are definitions updated automatically?
evidence_example: Endpoint protection console screenshot; patch/update policy; last malware scan results
evidence_description: Anti-malware is deployed on all workstations via managed AV but two older inventory laptops lack coverage.
finding_notes: Two Windows 7 inventory laptops (not on domain) are used for vendor portal access. No AV installed. High risk.

control_description: Procedures for monitoring log-in attempts and reporting discrepancies.
pharmacy_context: A technician's credential used at 3 AM when the store closed at 9 PM is an anomaly. PMS and Windows AD should both alert.
assessment_question: Are failed login attempts and off-hours access alerts reviewed and investigated?
evidence_example: SIEM/alert configuration; incident response ticket from a login anomaly; monthly anomaly summary
evidence_description: No SIEM exists. PMS does not send alerts. Windows logs are local only and not reviewed.
finding_notes: Without centralized logging or alerting the pharmacy would not detect credential compromise until a breach is reported.

control_description: Password management procedures for creating changing and safeguarding passwords.
pharmacy_context: Pharmacies often share generic logins ('Tech1' 'Tech2') or use sticky notes under keyboards. This is a common OCR finding.
assessment_question: Is there an enforced password policy (complexity rotation MFA) for all ePHI-accessing systems?
evidence_example: Password policy document; Group Policy / MDM settings; MFA enrollment dashboard
evidence_description: Password policy exists and is enforced on Windows domain but not on PMS. MFA is not implemented on any system.
finding_notes: PMS allows weak passwords and does not enforce rotation. No MFA for remote access or admin accounts.

control_description: Implement policies and procedures to address security incidents.
pharmacy_context: A lost backup tape ransomware on the PMS server or a technician emailing PHI to a personal Gmail are all security incidents requiring documented response.
assessment_question: Is there a documented Security Incident Response Plan covering identification containment eradication recovery and lessons learned?
evidence_example: Incident Response Plan; incident log (last 12 months); contact tree/escalation matrix
evidence_description: Incident Response Plan exists but was last updated in 2023. Contact list has outdated phone numbers for two vendors.
finding_notes: Plan exists but is stale. Two vendors on the contact tree were acquired and numbers changed. No annual tabletop exercise.

control_description: Identify and respond to suspected or known security incidents; mitigate harmful effects.
pharmacy_context: Tabletop exercise: 'PMS vendor reports ransomware in their cloud tenant affecting your patient data.' Can the PIC reach the Security Officer at 2 AM?
assessment_question: Has the organization responded to at least one simulated or real incident in the last 12 months to validate the IR plan?
evidence_example: Tabletop exercise after-action report; incident response drill schedule; post-mortem documentation
evidence_description: No tabletop exercise or incident drill has been conducted in the last 12 months. No real incidents requiring IR plan activation.
finding_notes: Last drill was March 2024. Staff turnover since then means most current employees have never practiced the plan.

control_description: Establish policies and procedures for responding to emergencies or other occurrences that damage systems containing ePHI.
pharmacy_context: If the PMS server goes down during a Saturday rush can the pharmacy still verify prescriptions and fill safely? Paper backups and downtime procedures must exist.
assessment_question: Does a Business Continuity / Disaster Recovery Plan exist and cover ePHI systems (PMS billing email)?
evidence_example: BCP/DRP document; downtime SOP; last annual DR test results
evidence_description: BCP exists and covers PMS but does not include the new insurance clearinghouse added in 2025. Downtime SOP exists.
finding_notes: New clearinghouse is not in the BCP. Downtime SOP is a single page and lacks detail for multi-day outages.

control_description: Data backup plan.
pharmacy_context: Pharmacies generate massive Rx data daily. An untested backup is a false hope. Verify a restore of a single patient profile was completed in the last quarter.
assessment_question: Are ePHI backups performed regularly tested for restorability and stored securely off-site or in encrypted cloud storage?
evidence_example: Backup schedule; encryption at-rest certificate; quarterly restore test log
evidence_description: Daily backups are performed to a local NAS and an encrypted cloud provider. However no restore test has been done in 8 months.
finding_notes: Backup verification was skipped due to staff shortage. The last successful restore test was September 2025.

control_description: Disaster recovery plan.
pharmacy_context: RTO of 4 hours means the pharmacy can be back on PMS by lunch if it fails at opening. RPO of 1 hour means losing at most 1 hour of Rx data.
assessment_question: Is there a documented Disaster Recovery Plan with RTO/RPO targets for ePHI systems?
evidence_example: DRP with RTO/RPO definitions; failover test results; alternative site agreement (if applicable)
evidence_description: DRP exists but RTO/RPO targets are not formally defined or tested. Failover procedures rely on a single IT vendor contact.
finding_notes: DRP states 'restore from backup' but does not define how long that takes or who does it if the IT vendor is unreachable.

control_description: Emergency mode operation plan.
pharmacy_context: If the insurance adjudication network is down the pharmacy can still fill prescriptions but must collect payment info securely for later billing. Paper logs must not leak PHI.
assessment_question: Are there procedures for operating in emergency mode (e.g. partial system failure network outage) while maintaining PHI protections?
evidence_example: Emergency mode SOP; paper-form security procedures; last emergency mode drill
evidence_description: Emergency mode SOP exists for PMS downtime but not for partial network failures (e.g. internet down but PMS up).
finding_notes: If internet is down the pharmacy cannot process insurance claims. Current SOP says 'call insurance later' but does not secure paper claim forms.

control_description: Testing and revision procedures.
pharmacy_context: New PMS version new insurance clearinghouse or a store remodel (new network layout) all trigger plan updates.
assessment_question: Are contingency plans tested annually and revised based on test findings system changes and business changes?
evidence_example: Annual test schedule; test results; plan revision history
evidence_description: No annual BCP/DR test has been performed. Plans have not been updated since 2023 despite system changes.
finding_notes: PMS was upgraded in 2024. Insurance clearinghouse changed in 2025. Neither event triggered plan updates.

control_description: Applications and data criticality analysis.
pharmacy_context: PMS is Tier 1. Inventory management is Tier 2. Marketing email list is Tier 3. This prioritization drives backup frequency and DR sequencing.
assessment_question: Has the organization identified which applications and data are critical to patient care and business operations and prioritized them in contingency planning?
evidence_example: Criticality matrix; application inventory with tiers; business impact analysis
evidence_description: No criticality analysis exists. All systems are treated equally in backup and DR planning.
finding_notes: The inventory laptop and the PMS server have the same backup frequency. The inventory system could be down for a day with minimal patient impact.

control_description: Perform periodic technical and nontechnical evaluations in response to environmental or operational changes affecting ePHI security.
pharmacy_context: An annual self-assessment using this exact toolkit meets the spirit of the requirement for a small pharmacy. Larger chains may layer a third-party audit.
assessment_question: Is there an annual evaluation program (internal audit gap assessment pen-test) assessing Security Rule compliance?
evidence_example: Annual evaluation report; pen-test findings; gap assessment (this artifact)
evidence_description: This gap assessment IS the evaluation for 2026. No third-party audit or pen-test has been conducted.
finding_notes: Internal evaluation only. No external validation. No vulnerability scanning or pen-testing budgeted for 2026.

control_description: Have contracts or other arrangements with business associates that establish permitted uses and disclosures and require safeguards.
pharmacy_context: Critical pharmacy BAs: PMS vendor insurance clearinghouse delivery service (if they see patient names/addresses) IT support company shredding vendor cloud backup provider.
assessment_question: Are Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) in place with all vendors who create receive maintain or transmit ePHI?
evidence_example: BAA inventory; sample executed BAA; vendor onboarding checklist requiring BAA before data sharing
evidence_description: BAAs are in place for PMS vendor insurance clearinghouse and shredding vendor. Missing for IT support company and delivery service.
finding_notes: IT support vendor (TechFix) has had admin access to PMS for 2 years without a BAA. Delivery service sees patient names but no BAA.

control_description: Document satisfactory assurances from business associates that they will appropriately safeguard ePHI.
pharmacy_context: A cloud backup vendor must encrypt data in transit and at rest. If they won't sign a BAA with security provisions they cannot handle pharmacy backups.
assessment_question: Do BAAs include language requiring the BA to comply with Security Rule safeguards and report breaches within a defined timeframe?
evidence_example: BAA language excerpts; vendor security questionnaire; SOC 2 report on file
evidence_description: Existing BAAs include general HIPAA language but lack specific security safeguard requirements and breach reporting SLAs.
finding_notes: BAA with insurance clearinghouse requires breach notification 'as soon as practicable' but defines no SLA (e.g. 24 hours).

control_description: If a business associate violates terms reasonable steps to cure; if unsuccessful terminate contract.
pharmacy_context: If the delivery company reports a lost manifest with patient names the pharmacy must document the incident request a root cause and consider switching vendors if recurrent.
assessment_question: Is there a documented process for monitoring BA compliance and escalating/remediating violations including contract termination?
evidence_example: BA monitoring procedure; violation log; contract termination checklist
evidence_description: No BA monitoring process exists. Compliance is assumed based on BAA signature alone. No annual vendor reviews.
finding_notes: Vendor compliance is not monitored. No violation log exists. There is no escalation path if a BA reports a breach.

control_description: Implement policies and procedures to limit physical access to electronic information systems and facilities while ensuring authorized access is allowed.
pharmacy_context: Server closet / network rack pharmacy back-office with dispensing terminals and vaccine refrigerator areas (which may have inventory systems) need controlled access.
assessment_question: Are there facility access controls (badge key biometric) for areas housing ePHI systems with an access log?
evidence_example: Access control policy; badge access logs; visitor sign-in sheets
evidence_description: Back office and server closet have keyed locks but no badge or biometric access. Key is kept in the manager's desk drawer.
finding_notes: Server closet key is on the same ring as the front door key. 6 staff members have copies. No access log is maintained.

control_description: Contingency operations — establish procedures allowing facility access in support of data restoration.
pharmacy_context: If the PMS server fails at 7 PM the on-call IT vendor needs after-hours access. An on-call pharmacist or manager must be able to grant it without compromising security.
assessment_question: Can authorized IT staff or a backup vendor access the facility after hours to perform emergency data restoration?
evidence_example: After-hours access SOP; on-call contact list; lockbox / smart-lock procedure
evidence_description: No after-hours access procedure exists for IT vendors. The PIC would need to drive to the store to unlock the door.
finding_notes: If PMS fails at 7 PM the PIC must physically come to the store. No lockbox smart lock or on-call security guard exists.

control_description: Facility security plan — safeguard the facility and equipment from unauthorized physical access tampering and theft.
pharmacy_context: Drive-thru windows are high-risk: audio systems capture patient names and birth dates. Cameras should cover drive-thru terminals but not capture screen contents.
assessment_question: Is there a facility security plan covering alarms cameras locks and environmental controls for ePHI areas?
evidence_example: Facility security plan; camera coverage map; alarm monitoring contract; last physical security walkthrough
evidence_description: Facility has alarm and cameras but no formal security plan. Cameras cover registers but not the back-office or server closet.
finding_notes: Alarm is monitored. Cameras cover front of house only. Server closet has no camera coverage. No annual physical security walkthrough.

control_description: Access control and validation procedures — control and validate a person's access to facilities based on role.
pharmacy_context: IT contractors servicing the router should receive a temp badge be escorted in the back office and sign an NDA before touching any system.
assessment_question: Are visitor and contractor access badges distinct from employee badges time-limited and escorted where required?
evidence_example: Badge types documented; visitor log; escort policy; contractor NDA on file
evidence_description: Visitors sign a paper log but no badges are issued. Contractors are not consistently escorted in the back office.
finding_notes: Last IT contractor (April 2026) was left alone in the back office for 20 minutes while staff handled a rush.

control_description: Maintenance records — document repairs and modifications to the physical components of a facility.
pharmacy_context: When the locksmith rekeys the pharmacy after a lost key incident the work order must be retained. When the camera system is upgraded the change is documented.
assessment_question: Are maintenance and modification activities for physical security components logged and retained?
evidence_example: Maintenance log; work orders; vendor invoices (redacted)
evidence_description: Maintenance work orders are kept for 1 year for tax purposes but not retained for 6 years as required by HIPAA.
finding_notes: Work orders are shredded after tax season. No separate maintenance log for security components exists.

control_description: Implement policies and procedures that specify proper use of workstations and access to ePHI.
pharmacy_context: Patient counseling terminals and drive-thru terminals must be positioned so patients in line or at the register cannot see the screen. Privacy filters are a cheap high-impact control.
assessment_question: Is there a Workstation Use Policy defining acceptable use screen privacy and physical arrangement to prevent unauthorized viewing?
evidence_example: Workstation Use Policy; workstation layout diagram; privacy filter installation record
evidence_description: Workstation Use Policy exists but does not address screen privacy or drive-thru terminal positioning. No privacy filters installed.
finding_notes: Drive-thru terminal is visible from the exterior window. Patients in line can read patient names on screen.

control_description: Implement physical safeguards for all workstations that access ePHI to restrict access to authorized users.
pharmacy_context: A dispensing terminal left unlocked while the pharmacist steps away for lunch break is a common physical vulnerability. Auto-lock after 5 minutes is the minimum.
assessment_question: Are workstations with ePHI access physically secured (cable locks locked office auto-lock) when unattended?
evidence_example: Physical security checklist; auto-lock Group Policy settings; cable lock inventory
evidence_description: Auto-lock is enabled on most workstations (15 min timeout) but not on the drive-thru terminal or counseling room tablet.
finding_notes: Drive-thru terminal has no auto-lock. Counseling tablet is sometimes left on the counter with patient profile visible.

control_description: Implement policies and procedures for the use and removal of hardware and electronic media.
pharmacy_context: USB drives used for backup old PMS terminals sent for recycling and fax machines (which store received images) must all be tracked until secure disposal.
assessment_question: Is there an asset inventory of all devices and media that store or process ePHI with ownership location and disposition tracking?
evidence_example: Asset inventory (redacted); media tracking log; device checkout procedure
evidence_description: No comprehensive asset inventory exists. Devices are tracked for accounting (depreciation) but not for security disposition.
finding_notes: Last PMS terminal was sent for recycling in 2024 with no documented data sanitization. Fax machines are not inventoried.

control_description: Disposal procedures — ensure ePHI is removed from electronic media before disposal or reuse.
pharmacy_context: When a pharmacy replaces an old PMS terminal the hard drive must be wiped or physically destroyed before the machine leaves the building.
assessment_question: Is there a documented media sanitization procedure (NIST SP 800-88 Clear/Purge/Destroy) before disposal or donation?
evidence_example: Sanitization policy; certificate of destruction from vendor; chain-of-custody log
evidence_description: Sanitization policy exists but is not consistently followed. No certificates of destruction are obtained from recyclers.
finding_notes: Policy says 'wipe drives' but the last two replacements were given to a local recycler with no verification.

control_description: Media re-use — ensure ePHI is removed before media is made available for re-use.
pharmacy_context: A backup drive from Store A should be fully wiped before being used as the new backup drive for Store B.
assessment_question: Before reusing hard drives USB drives or backup tapes is a verified wipe performed?
evidence_example: Wipe verification logs; drive re-use checklist; tool used (e.g. DBAN Blancco)
evidence_description: No media re-use procedure exists. Backup drives are reused without verification. USB drives are shared among stores.
finding_notes: Backup drives are rotated between stores with no wiping. A drive from Store 4421 was plugged into Store 4422 with old data intact.

control_description: Accountability — maintain a record of movements of hardware and electronic media.
pharmacy_context: Backup tapes or encrypted drives sent to off-site storage must be logged: date courier recipient expected return/destruction date.
assessment_question: Is there a chain-of-custody log for all ePHI-bearing media that leaves the facility?
evidence_example: Chain-of-custody log; courier receipts; off-site storage inventory
evidence_description: Chain-of-custody log exists for backup tapes sent to Iron Mountain but not for USB drives laptops or tablets that leave the facility.
finding_notes: Laptops taken home by managers and tablets used for off-site vaccination clinics have no chain-of-custody tracking.

control_description: Data backup and storage — create a retrievable exact copy of ePHI before equipment movement.
pharmacy_context: Before a store remodel moves the PMS server rack a full backup must be verified. After the move a spot-check restore validates data integrity.
assessment_question: Before moving or replacing servers/workstations with ePHI is a verified backup performed and tested?
evidence_example: Pre-move backup log; restore verification after move; change control ticket
evidence_description: Backups are performed before major moves but restore verification is not consistently done. Last move (2023) had no post-move verification.
finding_notes: Server was moved during 2023 remodel. Backup was taken but not tested after reconnection. No integrity issues found yet.

control_description: Implement technical policies and procedures to allow access only to persons or software programs granted access rights.
pharmacy_context: The PMS must support unique user IDs not shared 'pharmacy' or 'tech' accounts. Role-based menus (cashier vs. technician vs. pharmacist) must be enforced in software.
assessment_question: Are technical access controls (RBAC ACLs user authentication) enforced by the PMS and all ePHI-touching systems?
evidence_example: PMS user list showing unique IDs; role configuration screenshot; ACL review report
evidence_description: PMS enforces unique IDs but RBAC is not fully configured. The 'Inventory' role can still view patient names in reporting screens.
finding_notes: PMS roles are basic. Custom reports bypass role restrictions allowing inventory clerks to export patient lists.

control_description: Unique user identification — assign a unique name and/or number for identifying and tracking user identity.
pharmacy_context: Shared accounts break audit trails. If 5 technicians use 'Tech1' a breach investigation cannot determine which individual accessed a patient's profile.
assessment_question: Does every workforce member have a unique user ID for every ePHI system? Are shared accounts (e.g. 'frontdesk' 'admin') prohibited?
evidence_example: User ID policy; Active Directory / PMS user list; shared account remediation plan
evidence_description: Unique IDs are used on Windows domain and PMS but the fax machine uses a shared 'PharmacyFax' account. The Wi-Fi uses a shared WPA2 key.
finding_notes: Fax machine and network-attached printer use shared credentials. The wireless network password is known by former employees.

control_description: Emergency access procedure — establish procedures for obtaining necessary ePHI during an emergency.
pharmacy_context: If the PMS authentication server fails during a power outage a pharmacist must still be able to access patient allergy information. Break-glass accounts should be sealed logged and single-use.
assessment_question: Are there documented break-glass / emergency access procedures for when normal authentication is unavailable?
evidence_example: Break-glass policy; sealed envelope procedure; usage log; post-emergency review
evidence_description: No break-glass procedure exists. If PMS authentication fails there is no documented way to access patient data.
finding_notes: PMS vendor can reset admin password remotely but this takes 2-4 hours. No local break-glass account or sealed envelope exists.

control_description: Automatic logoff — implement electronic procedures that terminate an electronic session after a predetermined time of inactivity.
pharmacy_context: A drive-thru terminal or counseling room tablet left unlocked while the pharmacist steps away is a breach risk. Auto-logoff should be system-enforced not user-configurable.
assessment_question: Do all ePHI systems enforce automatic logoff after a defined period of inactivity (e.g. 5–15 minutes)?
evidence_example: PMS inactivity timeout settings; Windows screensaver/lock GPO; MDM policy for tablets
evidence_description: Windows domain workstations have 15-minute screensaver lock. PMS has no auto-logoff. Tablets have no MDM and no auto-lock.
finding_notes: PMS relies on users logging out manually. Counseling tablet has no screen lock. Drive-thru terminal never locks.

control_description: Encryption and decryption — implement a mechanism to encrypt and decrypt ePHI.
pharmacy_context: Pharmacy laptops taken home by the manager for after-hours inventory must have full-disk encryption. Insurance claims transmitted to the clearinghouse must use TLS 1.2 or higher.
assessment_question: Is ePHI encrypted at rest (databases backups laptops) and in transit (TLS 1.2+ VPN secure email)?
evidence_example: Encryption policy; BitLocker/FileVault/McAfee FDE reports; TLS scan results (SSL Labs); VPN configuration
evidence_description: PMS database is not encrypted at rest. Backups are encrypted. Laptops lack FDE. Insurance clearinghouse uses TLS 1.2.
finding_notes: PMS vendor claims database encryption is 'in development' for 2026 release. Manager laptop has no BitLocker.

control_description: Implement hardware software and/or procedural mechanisms to record and examine activity in information systems containing ePHI.
pharmacy_context: PMS audit trails should capture: Rx viewed Rx modified insurance claim submitted prescriber DEA lookup and inventory adjustment. Logs must be tamper-resistant.
assessment_question: Do ePHI systems generate audit logs for user access data modifications and failed authentication attempts?
evidence_example: Audit log sample (synthetic); SIEM configuration; log integrity check (checksum/hash chain)
evidence_description: PMS generates audit logs but they are not centralized. No log integrity checks (hashing) are performed. Logs can be deleted by admin.
finding_notes: PMS admin role can delete audit logs. No immutable log storage or WORM backup exists. No SIEM integration.

control_description: Implement mechanisms to authenticate ePHI and ensure it has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.
pharmacy_context: If a technician alters a patient's insurance ID to bill a different carrier the PMS should flag the change or require a supervisor override with a documented reason.
assessment_question: Are integrity controls (hashing digital signatures checksums version control) used for ePHI and audit logs?
evidence_example: Integrity policy; PMS change-control settings; database hashing configuration; backup integrity verification
evidence_description: PMS has field-level change logging but no cryptographic integrity checks. Audit logs are not hashed.
finding_notes: Change logs show who changed what but an attacker with DB access could alter history. No blockchain or Merkle tree used.

control_description: Mechanism to authenticate ePHI — electronic signatures or comparable mechanisms.
pharmacy_context: A pharmacist overriding a DUR (Drug Utilization Review) warning should require their own credentials not allow the technician to type the pharmacist's password.
assessment_question: For high-risk transactions (Rx overrides inventory adjustments prescriber additions) is there a secondary authentication or approval mechanism?
evidence_example: Override approval workflow; dual-control policy; e-signature configuration in PMS
evidence_description: PMS requires dual authentication for high-risk actions: Rx override requires pharmacist PIN. Inventory adjustment requires supervisor approval.
finding_notes: Controls are enforced in PMS. Two-person integrity for controlled substance inventory counts. Pharmacist PIN for DUR overrides.

control_description: Implement procedures to verify that a person or entity seeking access to ePHI is the one claimed.
pharmacy_context: Drive-thru terminals and counseling room tablets should not default to a logged-in state. Each user must authenticate individually.
assessment_question: Does every system with ePHI require authentication (password smart card biometrics) before granting access?
evidence_example: Authentication policy; MFA enrollment rate; smart card / badge reader inventory; PMS login screen photo
evidence_description: Windows and PMS require passwords. Tablets and fax machine do not. No MFA on any system. No biometrics.
finding_notes: Counseling tablet stays logged in as 'pharmacist' all day. Fax machine has no authentication. No MFA anywhere.

control_description: Implement technical security measures to guard against unauthorized access to ePHI transmitted over an electronic communications network.
pharmacy_context: The pharmacy's guest Wi-Fi must be segmented from the PMS network. Insurance claims and e-prescribing traffic must traverse encrypted tunnels.
assessment_question: Are network perimeter controls (firewall IDS/IPS VPN network segmentation) in place and regularly reviewed?
evidence_example: Network diagram (synthetic); firewall rule review; network segmentation test results; wireless security scan
evidence_description: Firewall exists but rules have not been reviewed in 18 months. Guest Wi-Fi is on the same VLAN as pharmacy workstations.
finding_notes: Guest Wi-Fi and pharmacy devices share 192.168.1.0/24. A compromised guest device could scan the PMS server.

control_description: Integrity controls — ensure ePHI is not improperly modified during transmission.
pharmacy_context: An e-prescription sent from the prescriber to the pharmacy should be digitally signed or transmitted over a trusted network (Surescripts) to prevent tampering.
assessment_question: Are integrity checks (TLS message authentication codes checksums) applied to all ePHI transmissions?
evidence_example: Surescripts / e-prescribing network agreement; TLS certificate inventory; message integrity check documentation
evidence_description: e-Prescribing uses Surescripts network with end-to-end integrity controls. Insurance claims use TLS 1.2 with certificate pinning.
finding_notes: Surescripts agreement on file. TLS 1.2 enforced by insurance clearinghouse. No plaintext PHI transmission detected.

control_description: Encryption — encrypt ePHI whenever deemed appropriate by the entity.
pharmacy_context: Emailing a patient's insurance card to the billing department must use encrypted email or a secure portal. Faxing PHI is still common but should be migrating to secure alternatives.
assessment_question: Is encryption applied to all ePHI transmissions outside the organization's trusted internal network?
evidence_example: Email encryption policy; secure portal URL; fax migration plan; TLS / IPsec tunnel documentation
evidence_description: Email is not encrypted. Fax is still used for 40% of prescriber communications. No secure portal exists.
finding_notes: Staff use personal Gmail for sending insurance forms to patients. Fax is unencrypted analog line. No secure portal.

control_description: Maintain written security policies and procedures including changes until 6 years after their last effective date.
pharmacy_context: An OCR audit may request policies from 4 years ago. Paper and electronic policy repositories must have 6-year retention and version control.
assessment_question: Are all security policies procedures and documentation retained for at least 6 years?
evidence_example: Policy retention schedule; document management system screenshot; version history sample
evidence_description: Policies are retained but version control is ad-hoc (file names with dates). No formal document management system.
finding_notes: Policies are on a shared drive with dated filenames. No check-in/check-out. No immutable archive. Risk of accidental deletion.

control_description: Documentation must be available to those responsible for implementing the procedures.
pharmacy_context: A new technician on Day 1 should be able to find the Password Policy Sanction Policy and Incident Response Plan without asking a supervisor.
assessment_question: Can workforce members easily access current security policies and procedures (intranet shared drive binder)?
evidence_example: Policy portal URL; shared drive path; printed policy binder location; new-hore orientation checklist referencing policies
evidence_description: All policies are on a shared drive with a shortcut on every workstation desktop. Printed binder is in the break room.
finding_notes: New-hire orientation includes a 10-minute walkthrough of the shared drive. Policies are updated quarterly and emailed.

control_description: Review documentation periodically and update as needed in response to environmental or operational changes.
pharmacy_context: A new PMS module for vaccine scheduling a store acquisition or an OCR guidance update all trigger policy review.
assessment_question: Are security policies reviewed at least annually and updated after significant incidents system changes or regulatory updates?
evidence_example: Annual review schedule; last review sign-off; change-triggered review log
evidence_description: Policies are reviewed annually but there is no change-triggered review process. New systems are added without policy updates.
finding_notes: Vaccine scheduling module was added in 2024. No policy updates were made to address new ePHI flows.

control_description: Time limit — retain documentation for 6 years from creation or last effective date.
pharmacy_context: Old printed Employee Handbooks and old policy PDFs on a shared drive must both be retained or purged according to a documented retention schedule.
assessment_question: Is the 6-year retention requirement enforced for both electronic and paper documentation?
evidence_example: Retention schedule; backup/archive policy; auto-purge rules for shared drives
evidence_description: Electronic retention is 6 years via backup. Paper retention is 3 years (tax record standard). No separate HIPAA retention for paper.
finding_notes: Paper employee handbooks are shredded after 3 years. This could violate 164.316(b)(2)(i) if audited.
